analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments first this morning in Lake Country of State against the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency. Mr. Bartow, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. G. Harris, please the Court. My argument will focus on the questions of whether there should be a per se agreement, according all compact created agencies, the status of states for the purpose of the 11th Amendment, without regard to their purpose, financing, function, or the relationship of the agency to the state. As subsidiary issues there under, whether under appropriate agencies, the compact agency under appropriate standards, the compact agency before the Court should be treated as a state, and further, whether the provisions of this compact have waived any claim of immunity. Also, my argument will focus on the question of whether or not the claims asserted under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983 are such that the 11th Amendment may be raised as a bar. In addition to the 11th Amendment issues, the petition raises the question of whether or not the members of the governing body of this agency should be accorded the absolute immunity which are accorded to members of Congress and members of state legislatures. Mr. G. Harris, please the question of what I would call the merits of your claim against the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency? Mr. G. with which we deal is known as the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency it is the product of an agreement between the states of California and Nevada whereby they created a regional agency with the power to regulate and control land use development and certain environmental factors in the Lake Tahoe Basin Congress gave its consent to the compact in December of 1969 the agency is controlled by a governing board consisting of 10 members none of whom are elected the TRPA was charged by the compact with adopting a regional land use plan and ordinances rules and policies to effectuate that plan its jurisdiction as I have said is limited to the Lake Tahoe Basin petitioners are owners of land in the Tahoe Basin a master plan had been approved by local governmental authorities for the development of their land subsequent thereto the TRPA enacted its plan and classified virtually all of petitioners property into a category known as general forest the permitted uses in that category were largely permitted uses the complaint alleged the taking without just compensation and a denial of due process under the fifth and fourteenth amendments as well as plans under similar provisions in the state agency's authority since it had not been granted condemnation powers, and as such would have been ultra-virus. But if the powers exercised are inflated to something like zoning authority, then that's another matter, isn't it? Well, in this Court's decision of last term, considering the ordinances of the City of New York, I think the Court has concluded that zoning in and of itself imposes regulatory uses which, if consistent with a due public purpose, can be appropriate, but there are out-of-limits even zoning costs. In this particular instance, there are both zoning regulations and classification of the land into permitted uses. We believe that the complaint, which is before the Court, presents the clearest of questions. Petitioners allege that... Presents what? The clearest of questions, Your Honor. In what respect? The complaint alleges that in this particular instance, the land is so ill-suited to the classification it was put into, that all value has been taken from it. Rather than... So that it's a taking? Yes, sir. A system on the taking? In addition, the District Court found that the individual members of the Tahoe governing body were protected in their discretionary acts with absolute immunity. The Court of Appeal... This case was consolidated with others in the Court of Appeals. The Court of Appeals ruled in its initial decision that the petitioners had stated the claim under the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause against the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency and against the individuals for injunctive and mandatory and declaratory relief. Because it was a case of use. Yes. That is the basis of their claim, that it was a taking involving a violation of the due process portion of the Fifth Amendment. The Court reasons that because Congress had given its consent to the compact, the compact had been transformed from two separate state laws into federal law for purposes of interpretation and ruled that the claim was based on the Fifth rather than the Fourteenth Amendment because it had become federal law. Well, just because federal law might govern wouldn't make it a federal action. Was the claim that this agency was a federal agency, action by the federal government, a taking by the federal government? No, the claim was under both the Fifth and the Fourteenth Amendment. Our position in the Court below and here has been that... Well, was the submission that a federal law governed it would be a Fifth Amendment question? The submission was that the act here constituted a violation of the guaranteed rights under the Constitution. That is to say, violations of the Fifth Amendment rights. By whom? By an agency which was not entitled to the protection of the Eleventh Amendment. An agency for these purposes, which may be seen generally. But the Fifth Amendment protects only against federal action, does it not? Yes, but the Fourteenth would protect against an action by this agency... If I were asking you what the claim was under the Fifth, why was there a claim that only the Fifth? Because the petitioners were unsure as to whether the plan could be under the Fifth or Fourteenth Amendment because of uncertainty as to whether or not the congressional consent would transform. Why are there a fact here? The state of California has a power of eminence domain, I'll take it. It does. And the state of Nevada has. It does. Could California have taken the action taken here with respect to the land lying within its borders? It is. It is under the power of eminence domain. It could, but in this particular instance, both states created an agency which they did not empower. And they didn't support to take it under the power of eminence domain. The agency did not support to take it under that power, did it? Correct. It did not have that power under either in Parliament. Would each of those two states, member states of the compact, have authority to exercise police power by way of zoning and land use? They would have such authority, but it's not traditional in either California or Nevada for states to exercise such zoning and regulatory power. Rather, it is more traditional for local government bodies such as cities and counties to exercise those powers. In this instance, the two constituent states created an agency with such powers, but without statutory power to affect a condemnation by eminence demand. Mr. Barber, I'm back up a minute. You said that when you filed a suit, you didn't know whether the agency of federal is free. What is a new demand yet? I think it has to be decided, doesn't it? I don't believe that it does have to be decided. I believe that this agency is not entitled to 11th Amendment protection in that although it may be, as a constituent portion of the state, a political subdivision. And therefore, the question of whether or not it's federal or state need not be decided, although the teachings of this court suggest that interpretation of the compact is in fact a federal question. The only issue before the court now is the issue of the 11th Amendment immunity of the agency. And since all constituent bodies of the state are not entitled to 11th Amendment, the question need not be reached. If this agency is more like a county in the city and more like a state, then the 11th Amendment would not protect it. But then it would have zoning powers, would it? Yes, it would, and in all fairness— And land use powers? Yes, and in all fairness, the provisions of this compact do in fact charge the agency with land use regulations. That was the whole purpose of creating it, wasn't it? Yes, it was. But it wouldn't have powers of condemnation? No, it would not. Or of taking? It would not and should not have under these circumstances. Well, in your inverse condemnation, too, in the federal law, isn't it the general requirement that unless Congress has authorized condemnation, your remedy is to enjoin the federal official who has gone on the property and effective the taking, rather than try to get damages? We have, in fact, included such claims in this complaint. For an injunction? For an injunction? We have included claims against the officers for an injunction and for declaratory relief that their actions are beyond their powers. But the issue still remains what is to happen as a petitioner in the interim period while he is contesting the validity of the agency and taking the actions it has taken. If, in fact, the agency has taken acts which are beyond its power and all petitioners' remedy will be if you tell them that they have stepped beyond their powers, then the attention of the courts will only be in pruning back regulation beyond the authority of the agency and they will have, in effect, a lease on petitioners' land while these questions are adjudicated. We believe that those claims for interim relief for monetary damages are appropriate under the Fifth Amendment's just compensation provision. Would you think you would be entitled to damages if there is no immunity? Simply from the fact that you need to be suspended for a period of time? I would believe that would be appropriate. You haven't sought that kind of damage here, have you? We have a general claim for damages. It is not limited in nature to interim relief as opposed to the ultimate value of the land. Our claims in this case are that if, in fact, there was a total taking, then the agency may be responsible for the full value of the land. If, in fact, they did not intend to take the land, it is only responsible for monetary relief for the interim period in which petitioner has been denied the use of his land while he seeks a remedy in the court to enjoin the agency from doing so further. Would that period cease as of the date an injunction was issued in your favor? I believe it would. I believe it would. The Court of Appeals granted a petition for rehearing and ruled, sui sponte, that although it had earlier decided that the court would have been denied the 11th Amendment's protection, it was intended to the 11th Amendment's protection. The decision of the Court of Appeals was premised upon its reading of this court's decision in Petty v. The Missouri-Tennessee Bridge Commission at 359 U.S. The Court of Appeals believes that that decision held that all compact agencies are the same as the states for 11th Amendment purposes. We believe a careful reading of that opinion will show that the author, Mr. Justice Douglas, in fact assumed arguendo for the purposes of that decision that the agency was, in fact, so protected by the 11th Amendment. In fact, the majority decision phrases the question as being one of whether or not there was a waiver, assuming arguendo that the entity was entitled to the protection. And three of the concurring justices concurred on an express stipulation that the court had not reached the constitutional question of whether or not the agency was, in fact, entitled to 11th Amendment protection. How would a waiver be relevant if there was nothing to waive? As a matter of analysis, it might not be relevant, Your Honor, but it was a way of sidestepping a more difficult question. And since the waiver appeared so clear to the court in that case, it is my view that the opinion did so in an appropriate fashion. Well, on your interpretation, isn't that somewhat like assuming without deciding that a court has jurisdiction, the court goes on to decide the case? Isn't a decision on that assumption, that argument or assumption about jurisdiction, a decision on the merits and a decision on jurisdiction? No, I believe the court always had jurisdiction to interpret the meaning of the compact, and the petty case makes that clear. The issue was not one of jurisdiction because the court had that jurisdiction to interpret its meaning. The issue was whether or not the court would also confront the question of whether all compact agencies, because they are created with the consent of Congress, are states for the purposes of 11th Amendment immunity. Now, we know from the teachings of this court, and particularly its decision in Mount Healthy v. Doyle at 429 United States reports, that not all portions of the state, not all subdivisions of the state, are entitled to 11th Amendment immunity. In that case, the court decided that a school board was not an arm of the state, but was more like a separate political subdivision, and as a consequence was not entitled to 11th Amendment immunity. We urge that the same view is appropriate when dealing with a compact created entity. The purpose of the compact clause, and Congress's express consent to the entry of states into compacts, was to protect the national interest to allow Congress to decide which compact should in fact be entered into, not to transform all agreements between states into the states themselves. If, in fact, all compact created entities are states for purposes of the 11th Amendment, it raises the question of whether or not a controversy between one of the creating states and the entity is such that it can only be brought in this court under its original and exclusive jurisdiction. No discernible reason has been advanced for singling out compact agencies from other political subdivisions of states for special protection. The arguments advanced by respondents that states would be unlikely to enter into compacts if by doing so they consented to federal jurisdiction. The argument is that under the court is always the final arbiter of the meaning of the compact. It also overlooks the fact that compacts can be created like this one, which expressly limits the responsibility of the constituent states and the power of the compact created agencies. In addition, we would urge the court to look to the intent of the parties in the creation of this compact. It is, after all, a contract between two states. Both the states of California and Nevada have argued in their briefs that the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency was not intended to have the 11th Amendment immunity of the states. In addition to the arguments urged before the court in their briefs, the provisions of the compact itself indicate the intent of the creating states that this particular agency not be entitled to assert their 11th Amendment immunity. Articles of the compact refer to the entity as a political subdivision. We know from the Mount Healthy decision that political subdivisions, if they are not compact created entities, are not entitled to 11th Amendment protection. A portion of the compact refers to jurisdiction in the federal courts. The jurisdiction of this particular agency is highly localized. Zoning and land use regulation is traditional, a local, not a state function. The authority to make rules is not limited by the veto power of the governors in this state. Look at that now. You say it's traditionally a state function. In neither of these states, California or Nevada, may they condemn land for state highways? In both states, I believe, the states have and do in fact exercise.ação incentive Woods distinguished from taking. Yes, Your Honor. Thank you for this court that they have no control over the compact agency which they have created. They have no veto power. The majority of the members of this compact agency and its governing body are appointed by local agencies, not by the governors of the respective states. Six of the ten members are, in fact, appointed by local counties and cities. As a consequence, the states do not control the agency which they have created. And by the state's campaign, the agency is considered by the Eighth Circuit in Petty and by the Second Circuit in Troutman. This lack of control by the constituent states shows that the compact has not created an arm of the states entitled to 11th Amendment immunity. What would you do about a home rule of city that under a state constitution has powers that can't be reached by the legislature? A home rule of city in my own state of California is, in fact, a separate political subdivision and would not be entitled to 11th Amendment immunity. So you would make the same argument with respect to them? I would. And you would say it's just like a state. No, I would say it is because, I misapprehended the court's question, excuse me. Control is an important factor in making a decision. In this particular instance, neither state has control. There may be instances... What about a home rule of city, then? Does it have 11th Amendment protection or doesn't it? I believe a home rule of city, if the state does not have control of it, should not have 11th Amendment protection. All of these provisions in the compact indicate the considered intent of the contracting party that the TRPA be a separate organ from state government. Lack of control is an important factor in making such a judgment. In addition, we believe the provisions of this compact, if there were, in fact, 11th Amendment immunity, have waived that immunity. We know that there can be such a waiver by this court's decision in Petty. We know by the court's decision in Edelman v. Jordan that such waivers should not be taken lightly. However, this compact has two interesting provisions, which we believe are analogous to those in Petty. It refers, in the compact language of Section 6b, to jurisdiction in the federal courts. It states as follows. Each such action shall be brought in a court of the state where the violation is committed, or where the property affected by a civil action is situated, unless the action is brought in a federal court. For this purpose, the agency shall be deemed a political subdivision of both the state of California and the state of Nevada. It refers expressly to federal court's jurisdiction. In addition, the congressional consent, which was also relied upon by the court in Petty, is, in our view, equally as broad. It provides that nothing in the compact should in any way affect the powers, rights, or obligations of the United States, or the applicability of any law or regulation of the United States in, over, or to the region. The only distinguishing factor in the consent provision in the Petty case was a specific reference to the courts of the United States. We believe that this provision is even more encompassing because it refers to all of the rights, powers, and obligations of the United States. Brief states that the states are not responsible for the debt of the agency. How is the agency financed? The agency has the power to call upon local counties for a fixed amount of funding in each fiscal year, as it presently stands $150,000. If the agency is to receive additional funds, it must rely on the largesse of the constituent states or perhaps grants and subventions from other agencies. The compact also provides that the state shall not be responsible for obligations created by the agency and limits the power of the agency in that respect. The other issue raised by the petition is whether or not the members of the governing body of this agency should be entitled to absolute immunity. The Court of Appeals ruled that to the extent that members of the body might be acting in part in a legislative function, they would be so entitled to absolute immunity. The teachings of this Court's decision indicate that absolute immunity has heretofore in the legislative sphere only been granted to members of Congress and members of state legislators, not to lower bodies. In the absence of the traditional safeguards, which were relied upon in this Court in the Butts decision last term, to extend immunity to those acting in a judicial function, it should not be done. In this particular instance, there are none of the traditional safeguards which apply to an ordinary legislature. The members of the governing body are not elected and called upon to justify their acts periodically. There is no established practice or rules of discipline in this body that would, in fact, allow the body to police itself and its members. Are the members appointed by the governors? A portion of the members are. Each governor has the right to appoint one member. There is also another member from each state who serves by reason of its classification as director of natural resources in each state. So four of the ten members are, in fact, either appointed or state officers. The remaining six officers are designated by reason of their service on local agencies such as counties and cities. By whom? By those local agencies. Well, then there's indirect public responsibility in each case, isn't there, with respect to some of the governors and with respect to some of the local agencies? Yes, but I believe that it is too indirect, Your Honor. In this instance, they would be serving in two functions. And they would not be called upon at an election with respect to whether or not they served as a good city councilman to also be responsible for their decisions as a member of this compact agency, since it is a broader function. Mr. Marshall, just a fact. You're arguing the immunity now? I am. I take it the Court of Appeals ruled on whether there was a cause of action under the 5th or the 14th or both, either one? It ruled that there was a cause of action under both the 5th and 14th Amendment and the 2nd decision. Now, I take it that there's been no cause of action? There has not. Is it your position? And yet the respondents argue is their first point that the Court of Appeals aired in holding there was a cause of action. That is correct. Do you think that issue is properly here? I do not believe it is properly here. I believe that issue goes only to the question of remedy. And in fact, what it would do would... Well, yes, but why shouldn't we be able to consider it? Let's assume that if we ruled in their favor, the case would be over. No, it would not be over to the extent we have stated claims against the individuals with respect to our claims for injunctive and declaratory relief. And as a consequence... Well, it would be over against the agency. It would be over against the agency. And we wouldn't have to consider some of the questions you've been arguing. Yes, that is true. Now, apparently the Court of Appeals felt that way, too, or it wouldn't have reached the cause of action issue. Ahead of immunity and ahead of the 11th Amendment jurisdictional questions. Yes, but I believe the question really that should be addressed is whether or not we have an appropriate record for this Court to determine such an important question. We come before you on a motion to dismiss... Well, the Court of Appeals thought it did. And it wouldn't expand the relief that the agency got before the Court of Appeals. The Court of Appeals did, in fact, reduce the relief it had granted against the agency. It originally had granted relief and then found that it could avoid that question by finding that 11th Amendment immunity applied. But what the Court would be doing by sidestepping the 11th Amendment immunity question would, on a very sparse record, in my view, be confronting a far more difficult question. That is whether... But let's assume that we disagreed with you on... If we agree with you, then where do we go? If we agree with you and there's no 11th Amendment immunity, where do we go then? Then the case would be remanded to the District Court for development of the facts and the records. And, in fact, we would proceed forward on the court based on the Fifth Amendment. You would argue that the respondents, then, cannot have us review the cause of action relief? I would so argue because it would not support the decision of the Court of Appeals. Well, it would, though, as far as the agency is concerned. Well, it would as far as the agency, but that goes to the agency and the agency alone. But it would not terminate the case because our claims against the individuals would survive for purposes of injunctive and mandatory relief. Well, then, at least the agency is entitled to have the Court of Appeals affirmed on a separate ground, is it not? The agency has made that claim. And I can see that... I can see... You're entitled. It's just you were to agree with all of its contentions as a matter of procedure. I'm not... We're not saying that they're right, but it's just a question of whether we're entitled or whether it be... Whether pre-dentary or even pre-dentary... I believe that... That, in fact, the Court can, under its prior decision, reach the cause of action, but it would be inappropriate on this record. What would be the relief against the individuals in that certain standard? The relief against the individuals would be both injunctive and, in fact, monetary. And what? And monetary to the extent that we seek interim relief with regard to what has happened to the property in the interim. Well, what cause of action is it? Is it a different cause of action against the individuals? No, the same cause of action against the individuals. What if we ruled the Court of Appeals was wrong on its cause of action ruling? It would go only to remedies to the individuals. If they were wrong with regard to the Bivin Bishop, in fact, there would be no monetary relief available against the individuals as well. Or injunctive. I believe that the constitutional... You still have to have a cause of action to get an injunction. Yes, we still have to have a cause of action, but the Bivin's claim, and in our view the constitutional claim, for purposes of determining whether there has been a taking or not, are different. There has, in fact, been, with regard to the immunity question, a traditional reluctance to expand absolute immunity, because qualified immunity in itself is ordinarily sufficient. It protects appropriate government actions. Mr. Rosten. Mr. Rosten. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, I would like to primarily address, in my portion of the argument, the question of the appropriate remedy in this case. Initially, I think the brief iteration of our view of the facts is in order. The zoning of this property is conservation reserve, which zoning permits development in accordance with a specific plan, a plan that is submitted, a master plan detailing, particularly on large parcels, the development which is desired on that parcel. The record of this case reveals that that specific plan was solicited by the governing body of TRPA at the time. This property was zone conservation reserve, and that no such application has been received. I believe it is also important to focus down to the fact that when we deal with appropriate remedies, as the issue is framed before this Court, and is monetary relief appropriate, principally we're talking about individuals. Individuals. Are those individuals responsible monetarily for their legislative acts? The specific individuals before this Court are the governing body members of the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency. Those individuals are sued for their specifically authorized act, specifically authorized by the compact, of adopting a general plan and a land use ordinance. It's not just that it's specifically authorized, it's specifically required. The compact in Article 5 tells the governing body members, thou shalt adopt a general plan. In Article 6, the compact tells the governing body members, thou shalt adopt a land use ordinance. So we have not just authorized, we have required legislative act. The government members, and the government, and the government, and the government, and the government, and the government, and the government, and the government, in great detail, specifies and constitutes the governing body. It's not left to move here. It's not left to move here. Are members of the zoning body, or any zoning body within the states, subject to liability, or are they immune? They're absolutely immune, under the law of both the state of California, and the state of Nevada. The pertinent authority is cited in my brief. Mr. Rolson, supposing that this compact had authorized the Regional Planning Authority to promulgate a criminal code, and the individual members of the governing body promulgated a code that said anyone caught, shop, let things should be taken out to the nearest tree and hung. Do you think the fact that the compact authorized the promulgation of a criminal code would completely immunize the members? Insofar as they are undertaking legislative acts, yes. I think it's important in responding to your question to note that we're dealing with a very, very significant difference when we talk about legislative acts as compared to executive acts. This court had before it earlier this term, butts versus economy, which counsel for the petitioners addressed. When you talk about executive acts, you're talking about a much more channelized area of responsibility. You wouldn't call the fellow who threw the rope over the tree limb a legislator, would you? I certainly would not, John. Oh, well, that's the... And apparently there's conduct in this case other than legislating. The only question before this court, though, Your Honor, as framed by the petition, or not the only question, but the only question on this issue, specifically as framed by the petition, is there absolute immunity for legislative acts, period. No one, neither petitioners nor respondents, have dealt with a non-legislative act. When you're dealing with executive acts, it seems to me you're dealing with a much more channelized area. Certainly there is discretion. If you have discretion within the law, principally, thou shalt enforce this area of the law. The eminent function of the... There are no such parameters for legislators at all. You have an area in which you may act. A broad area. The wisdom, the collective wisdom of whether that law is reasonable or necessary is up for the legislature to decide. Further, an executive official, unlike a legislator, is much more subject and much more continuously subject to the control and supervision of the judiciary, unlike what is typical of a legislator. Mr. Wilson, you mentioned earlier about how carefully they spelled out all these requirements, you put them. The action they should take, and I think you said they spelled it out in very great detail. But they didn't touch the immunity, did they? They did not try. They coded. But they did. Where do you get the immunity from? The state immunity. Well, I think this court in its prior decisions has recognized an absolute immunity for legislative acts. We can go to Tinney v. Brandho, Joe v. McMillan, the Gravel case. In those cases, this court manifestly was dealing with state and national legislators. What we're essentially asking is that the immunity... Do you think that this is on the same level as the governor or the legislature of Nevada? I'm sorry, Your Honor. This Tahoe Regional Planning Agency, is that on the level of the governor or the state legislature? Of the state legislature, Your Honor. It's on the same level. It's dealing with problems... How did it get there? It's not elected? Well, six... It's not elected. No. Six of the... But it gets an immunity to an officer that's not elected. He's appointed. I can't just pick up immunity like that. Well, it depends on whether you're examining immunity from the level of the actor of the task performed. In Butts v. Economist, this court spoke up. The level of the actor, the fact that some of these individuals, the Fendants in that case, were performing a judicial role. They were not, by any means, a court. Oh, you're talking about another case. I'm talking about another case. But I think it depends principally on the type of act that you're performing. What can they do in the name of the state? What can this Tahoe Regional Planning Agency do in the name of the state? Well, it's dealing with problems that the needed state can solve singly in the area of land use and environmental control. In the name of the state? Not in the name of the state, I guess. Well, my question was, what can they do in the name of the state? Not in the name of the state itself. It can do nothing.
